summary: I worry a rushed 2030 ban will hit people like me on modest incomes who may not afford an electric car or have easy access to charging, particularly older people in older homes or rural North West areas. I want cleaner air and local green jobs, but I need clear, reliable plans and funding that actually reach ordinary households before I’d support such a firm deadline.

Hearing this makes me see the benefits — cleaner air, lower running costs, new local jobs, and protection from fuel price swings — and I’m broadly supportive. But making the ban “fair” is crucial: I need reassurance that charging, home retrofits, and good public transport will reach people like me in older homes and rural areas, and a firm 2030 deadline feels rushed without clear, reliable plans and targeted support for modest-income households, even if funded by big corporations.

Reading that message makes me more convinced a 2030 ban is the bold, necessary government move we need to improve air quality and public health, especially near schools, while creating green jobs—provided it’s tied to practical support like free buses, grants, charging infrastructure and insulation so the costs aren’t unfairly shifted onto low‑income households. At the same time I worry about trade‑offs — whether charging and insulation can roll out fast enough, whether grants and scrappage schemes will be sufficient for working families, tradespeople and rural communities, and whether the deadline gives small businesses enough time to adapt — so I insist the transition must be genuinely well‑funded, timely and fair.

Reading that message increases my worries about the real-world impacts of a 2030 ban — I’m more aware of practical problems for rural residents, tradespeople, and small businesses, and I hear fears about costs, insurance, and replacing serviceable vehicles, so I believe any strong environmental policy must be paired with funded, targeted support (scrappage grants, rapid on‑street and rural charging, help for small firms). 

At the same time, I remain convinced a 2030 ban could bring big environmental and social benefits — cleaner air, lower running costs, and green jobs — but I’ll only fully back a firm deadline if the government commits to and delivers concrete measures, clear funding, and guarantees to protect vulnerable groups and rural economies during the transition.
